claim: DTD acts on achiral glycine, in addition to D-amino acids, attached to tRNA.
source: D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylase (DTD) acts on achiral glycine, in addition to D-amino acids, attached to tRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about DTD's activity.

claim: DTD clears non-cognate Gly-tRNAAla with 1000-fold higher efficiency than its activity on Gly-tRNAGly.
source: We have recently shown that this activity enables DTD to clear non-cognate Gly-tRNAAla with 1000-fold higher efficiency than its activity on Gly-tRNAGly, indicating tRNA-based modulation of DTD (Pawar et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Pawar et al., 2017).

claim: The tRNA's discriminator base predominantly accounts for the activity difference between DTD on Gly-tRNAAla and Gly-tRNAGly.
source: Here, we show that tRNA's discriminator base predominantly accounts for this activity difference and is the key to selection by DTD.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The uracil discriminator base serves as a negative determinant that prevents Gly-tRNAGly misediting by DTD.
source: Accordingly, the uracil discriminator base, serving as a negative determinant, prevents Gly-tRNAGly misediting by DTD and this protection is augmented by EF-Tu.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical assays showing differential DTD activity on tRNAs with different discriminator bases.

claim: EF-Tu augments the protection of Gly-tRNAGly from DTD misediting.
source: Accordingly, the uracil discriminator base, serving as a negative determinant, prevents Gly-tRNAGly misediting by DTD and this protection is augmented by EF-Tu.
evidence: This is supported by competition experiments between EF-Tu and DTD shown in Figure 3.

claim: Eukaryotic DTD has inverted discriminator base specificity compared to bacterial DTD.
source: Intriguingly, eukaryotic DTD has inverted discriminator base specificity and uses only G3•U70 for tRNAGly/Ala discrimination.
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical assays using mouse DTD on bacterial tRNAs with different discriminator bases.

claim: Eukaryotic DTD uses only G3•U70 for tRNAGly/Ala discrimination.
source: Intriguingly, eukaryotic DTD has inverted discriminator base specificity and uses only G3•U70 for tRNAGly/Ala discrimination.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis showing both eukaryotic tRNAGly and tRNAAla have A73, and biochemical data showing ~10-fold discrimination.

claim: DTD prevents alanine-to-glycine misincorporation in proteins rather than only recycling mischarged tRNAAla.
source: Moreover, DTD prevents alanine-to-glycine misincorporation in proteins rather than only recycling mischarged tRNAAla.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the GFP-based reporter assay showing fluorescence in dtd knockout cells.

claim: DTD exerts strong selection pressure on bacterial tRNAGlys to retain a pyrimidine discriminator code.
source: Overall, the study reveals the unique co-evolution of DTD and discriminator base, and suggests DTD's strong selection pressure on bacterial tRNAGlys to retain a pyrimidine discriminator code.
evidence: This is inferred from the bioinformatic analysis showing invariant U73 in bacterial tRNAGly and the biochemical data on DTD specificity.

claim: A compromise in editing leads to serious pathologies including neurodegeneration in mouse, and even cell death.
source: A compromise in editing leads to serious pathologies including neurodegeneration in mouse, and even cell death (Bacher et al., 2005; Bullwinkle et al., 2014; Karkhanis et al., 2007; Korencic et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014; Moghal et al., 2016; Nangle et al., 2002; Roy et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: DTD specifically decouples wrongly acylated D-amino acids from tRNAs.
source: Among these proofreading factors, D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylase (DTD) is the one that specifically decouples wrongly acylated D-amino acids from tRNAs (Calendar and Berg, 1967; Soutourina et al., 1999; 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational studies on DTD.

claim: DTD is an RNA-based catalyst that uses an invariant Gly-cisPro motif as a 'chiral selectivity filter'.
source: Our studies have shown that DTD is an RNA-based catalyst that uses an invariant Gly-cisPro motif as a 'chiral selectivity filter' to achieve substrate chiral specificity only through rejection of L-amino acid from the active site, thereby leading to Gly-tRNAGly misediting (Ahmad et al., 2013; Routh et al., 2016; Routh and Sankaranarayanan, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: DTD achieves substrate chiral specificity only through rejection of L-amino acid from the active site.
source: Our studies have shown that DTD is an RNA-based catalyst that uses an invariant Gly-cisPro motif as a 'chiral selectivity filter' to achieve substrate chiral specificity only through rejection of L-amino acid from the active site, thereby leading to Gly-tRNAGly misediting (Ahmad et al., 2013; Routh et al., 2016; Routh and Sankaranarayanan, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mechanistic studies.

claim: G3•U70 is a determinant for DTD but enhances DTD's activity by only about 10-fold.
source: G3•U70, the universal tRNAAla-specific determinant for AlaRS, is also a determinant for DTD. However, it enhances DTD's activity by only about 10-fold (Pawar et al., 2017), leaving the 100-fold difference in activity unaccounted for.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and sets up the motivation for the current study.

claim: Bacterial tRNAGly, tRNAHis and tRNACys have a pyrimidine as N73, while the rest of the tRNAs including tRNAAla have a purine at that position.
source: Surprisingly, bacterial tRNAGly, tRNAHis and tRNACys have a pyrimidine as N73, while the rest of the tRNAs including tRNAAla have a purine at that position (Figure 1a,c; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis of 2,671,763 tRNA sequences shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: The second base pair position is not conserved among different tRNAs on which DTD is known to act with similar efficiency.
source: However, this is not likely to affect DTD's activity because the second base pair position is not conserved among different tRNAs (e.g., tRNAPhe/Tyr/Trp/Asp) on which DTD is known to act with similar efficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Calendar and Berg, 1967; Soutourina et al., 1999; 2000).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and citations to previous studies on DTD substrates.

claim: EcDTD has nearly 100-fold higher activity on Gly-tRNAGly(U73A) or Gly-tRNAGly(U73G) compared to its activity on wild-type Gly-tRNAGly.
source: Strikingly, biochemical assays showed that DTD from E. coli (EcDTD) deacylates Gly-tRNAGly(U73A) or Gly-tRNAGly(U73G) at 0.1 nM, whereas it shows similar activity on Gly-tRNAGly at 10 nM (Figure 2a,c,d). Thus, EcDTD has nearly 100-fold higher activity on Gly-tRNAGly(U73A) or Gly-tRNAGly(U73G) compared to its activity on the wild-type substrate.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by biochemical assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: EcDTD's activity on Gly-tRNAGly(U73C) is similar to that on wild-type Gly-tRNAGly.
source: In the case of Gly-tRNAGly(U73C), EcDTD's activity at 10 nM is similar to that on Gly-tRNAGly at the same concentration, thus displaying comparable efficiencies for both substrates (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: N73 is a key element on tRNA that dictates the efficiency of DTD.
source: This clearly demonstrates that N73 is a key element on tRNA that dictates the efficiency of DTD, and purine as N73 is the preferred base for the enzyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the biochemical data showing differential DTD activity based on N73 identity.

claim: Purine as N73 is the preferred base for bacterial DTD.
source: This clearly demonstrates that N73 is a key element on tRNA that dictates the efficiency of DTD, and purine as N73 is the preferred base for the enzyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the biochemical data showing higher DTD activity on purine-containing N73 mutants.

claim: All reported substrates of DTD (D-Tyr-tRNATyr, D-Phe-tRNAPhe, D-Trp-tRNATrp and D-Asp-tRNAAsp) have purine as N73.
source: Our data is further strengthened by the fact that all the reported substrates of DTD, namely D-Tyr-tRNATyr, D-Phe-tRNAPhe, D-Trp-tRNATrp and D-Asp-tRNAAsp, have purine as N73 (Figure 1c; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Calendar and Berg, 1967; Soutourina et al., 1999; 2000).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: N73 has a stronger influence on DTD than G3•U70.
source: This also shows that N73 has a stronger influence on DTD than G3•U70 (which creates only about 10-fold difference) and it can majorly account for the observed 1000-fold difference in DTD's activity on Gly-tRNAGly and Gly-tRNAAla (Pawar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the ~100-fold effect of N73 to the ~10-fold effect of G3•U70.

claim: EcDTD's activity on Gly-tRNAGly(U73A/C70U) at 0.01 nM is comparable to that on Gly-tRNAAla, and is nearly 1000-fold higher than its activity on wild-type Gly-tRNAGly.
source: Biochemical assays showed that EcDTD's activity on Gly-tRNAGly(U73A/C70U) at 0.01 nM is comparable to that on Gly-tRNAAla, and is nearly 1000-fold higher than its activity on wild-type Gly-tRNAGly (Figure 2a,e,f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: N73 and G3•U70 have an additive effect on DTD's activity.
source: This unambiguously proves the additive effect of N73 and G3•U70 in modulating bacterial DTD's activity, wherein N73 plays the major role.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the double mutant showing the combined ~1000-fold effect.

claim: Just two point mutations in the acceptor stem are necessary and sufficient to completely switch the specificity of tRNAGly to tRNAAla.
source: More importantly, it shows that just two point mutations in the acceptor stem are necessary and sufficient to completely switch the specificity of tRNAGly to tRNAAla, one which is an anti-determinant in tRNAGly and the other a positive determinant in tRNAAla.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the U73A/C70U double mutant behaving like tRNAAla.

claim: Functionally important interactions of DTD are confined only to the acceptor stem of tRNA.
source: These results also clearly establish that functionally important interactions of DTD are confined only to the acceptor stem of tRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that only acceptor stem mutations are sufficient to switch specificity.

claim: EF-Tu confers protection on Gly-tRNAGly from DTD's unwarranted activity.
source: Our previous work had shown that elongation factor thermo unstable (EF-Tu) confers protection on Gly-tRNAGly from DTD's unwarranted activity (Routh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: tRNA elements on TΨC arm are known to be responsible for EF-Tu binding.
source: tRNA elements on TΨC arm are known to be responsible for EF-Tu binding (LaRiviere et al., 2001; Sanderson and Uhlenbeck, 2007a; Schrader et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and biochemical studies.

claim: N73 mutation in tRNAGly is not expected to alter the binding affinity of Gly-tRNAGly to EF-Tu.
source: Hence, N73 mutation in tRNAGly is not expected to alter the binding affinity of Gly-tRNAGly to EF-Tu.
evidence: This is inferred from the knowledge that EF-Tu binds the TΨC arm, not the discriminator base.

claim: The protection offered by EF-Tu to Gly-tRNAGly against EcDTD is less than 10-fold.
source: In the absence of EF-Tu, EcDTD acts on Gly-tRNAGly at 10 nM, while the presence of EF-Tu protects Gly-tRNAGly from 10 nM EcDTD. The substrate is, however, completely deacylated by 100 nM EcDTD even in the presence of EF-Tu. Thus, the protection offered by EF-Tu to Gly-tRNAGly against EcDTD is less than 10-fold (Figure 3a), which is in agreement with our previous study (Routh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by competition experiments shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Irrespective of the identity of N73, EF-Tu offers only about 10-fold protection.
source: In the case of Gly-tRNAGly(U73A), EcDTD's activity without EF-Tu is at 0.1 nM, while in the presence of EF-Tu, similar activity is observed at 1 nM (Figure 3b). Hence, irrespective of the identity of N73, EF-Tu offers only about 10-fold protection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by competition experiments with the U73A mutant shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The 100-fold difference in the activity of EcDTD on Gly-tRNAGly(U73A) and wild-type Gly-tRNAGly is maintained even in the presence of EF-Tu.
source: Furthermore, the 100-fold difference in the activity of EcDTD on Gly-tRNAGly(U73A) and wild-type Gly-tRNAGly is maintained even in the presence of EF-Tu.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the competition experiments in Figure 3a and 3b.

claim: EF-Tu has no preference for N73.
source: These findings clearly demonstrate that EF-Tu has no preference for N73, and it is DTD's differential activity that predominantly determines the fate of the substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistent ~10-fold protection by EF-Tu regardless of N73 identity.

claim: DTD's differential activity predominantly determines the fate of the substrate.
source: These findings clearly demonstrate that EF-Tu has no preference for N73, and it is DTD's differential activity that predominantly determines the fate of the substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing N73-dependent DTD activity differences are maintained in the presence of EF-Tu.

claim: EF-Tu augments the protection of Gly-tRNAGly primarily/majorly conferred by U73.
source: Thus, EF-Tu augments the protection of Gly-tRNAGly primarily/majorly conferred by U73, that is the enhancement in protection of Gly-tRNAGly by EF-Tu is consequential only if the substrate harbors U73.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined effects of U73 and EF-Tu shown in the competition experiments.

claim: Cellular DTD levels must be tightly regulated.
source: Nevertheless, cellular DTD levels must be tightly regulated because DTD overexpression has been shown to cause toxicity (Routh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work showing DTD overexpression toxicity.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type DTD causes complete depletion of Gly-tRNAGly.
source: In case of mutant DTD overexpression, the aminoacylated fraction is about 80% of the total tRNAGly pool which is similar to empty vector control. By contrast, overexpression of wild-type DTD causes complete depletion of Gly-tRNAGly.
evidence: This is demonstrated by northern blotting analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The toxicity caused by DTD overexpression is linked to the depletion of cellular Gly-tRNAGly levels.
source: These data are suggestive that the toxicity caused by DTD overexpression is linked to the depletion of cellular Gly-tRNAGly levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the northern blotting data showing Gly-tRNAGly depletion upon DTD overexpression.

claim: Both tRNAGly and tRNAAla in Archaea and Eukarya harbor A73.
source: Intriguingly, our bioinformatic analysis also revealed that the dichotomy of N73 seen in bacterial tRNAGly and tRNAAla is lacking in Archaea and Eukarya, that is both tRNAGly and tRNAAla in Archaea and Eukarya harbor A73 (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Archaea lacks canonical DTD.
source: Thus, we envisaged that the difference in eukaryotic DTD's activity on eukaryotic Gly-tRNAGly and Gly-tRNAAla will be only about 10-fold due to G3•U70 in tRNAAla (notably, Archaea lacks canonical DTD and hence the problem of discrimination does not arise at all).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about archaeal systems.

claim: MmDTD acts on Gly-(Mm)tRNAGly and Gly-(Mm)tRNAAla at 100 nM and 10 nM, respectively.
source: Biochemical assays revealed that MmDTD acts on Gly-(Mm)tRNAGly and Gly-(Mm)tRNAAla at 100 nM and 10 nM, respectively (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical assays shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: G3•U70 recognition by DTD is conserved even in Eukarya.
source: These results clearly show that G3•U70 recognition by DTD is conserved even in Eukarya, contributing about 10-fold discrimination between eukaryotic tRNAGly and tRNAAla.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ~10-fold difference in MmDTD activity on mouse tRNAGly vs tRNAAla.

claim: G3•U70 is the only available tRNA element that enables distinction between eukaryotic tRNAGly and tRNAAla by eukaryotic DTD.
source: They also demonstrate that G3•U70 is the only available tRNA element that enables distinction between eukaryotic tRNAGly and tRNAAla by eukaryotic DTD.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that both eukaryotic tRNAs have A73, leaving only G3•U70 as a distinguishing feature.

claim: Other mechanisms are possibly operating in eukaryotes to enhance the discrimination between Gly-tRNAGly and Gly-tRNAAla.
source: These findings further suggest that other mechanisms are possibly operating in eukaryotes to enhance the discrimination between Gly-tRNAGly and Gly-tRNAAla, as discussed later.
evidence: This is speculated based on the limited discrimination provided by G3•U70 alone in eukaryotes.

claim: MmDTD acts on U73-containing wild-type Gly-(Ec)tRNAGly at a concentration of 0.1 nM while it acts on Gly-(Ec)tRNAGly(U73A) mutant with comparable efficiency at a concentration of 10 nM.
source: MmDTD acts on U73-containing wild-type Gly-(Ec)tRNAGly at a concentration of 0.1 nM while it acts on Gly-(Ec)tRNAGly(U73A) mutant with comparable efficiency at a concentration of 10 nM, thus displaying a 100-fold reduction in activity compared to the wild-type substrate (Figure 3e,f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by biochemical assays shown in Figure 3e,f.

claim: Eukaryotic DTD has switched its N73 specificity/preference from purine to pyrimidine compared to bacterial DTD.
source: The data indicate that N73 does affect eukaryotic DTD but the specificity/preference has switched from purine to pyrimidine.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MmDTD showing higher activity on U73-containing tRNA than A73-containing tRNA.

claim: Bacterial DTD prefers purine while eukaryotic DTD prefers pyrimidine as N73.
source: Therefore, eukaryotic DTD is equally modulated by N73 like its bacterial counterpart, but has inverted N73 specificity, that is bacterial DTD prefers purine while eukaryotic DTD prefers pyrimidine as N73
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing bacterial and eukaryotic DTD activities on tRNAs with different N73.

claim: Mild overexpression of eukaryotic DTD from Plasmodium falciparum creates more cellular toxicity when compared to that of EcDTD.
source: this provides a rationale as to why a mild overexpression of eukaryotic DTD from Plasmodium falciparum (PfDTD; eukaryotic DTD) creates more cellular toxicity when compared to that of EcDTD (Routh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and explained by the inverted N73 specificity.

claim: Eukaryotic DTD has co-evolved with N73 like bacterial DTD.
source: These findings clearly establish that eukaryotic DTD has also co-evolved with N73 like bacterial DTD, thereby helping to relieve the selection pressure of keeping U/C73 in eukaryotic tRNAGly, as further explained later.
evidence: This is inferred from the inverted N73 specificity of eukaryotic DTD matching the change in eukaryotic tRNAGly N73.

claim: None of the U/C73-containing eukaryotic tRNAs is known to be mischarged with glycine or corresponding D-amino acids.
source: Nevertheless, since none of the U/C73-containing eukaryotic tRNAs (Figure 1c) is known to be mischarged with glycine or corresponding D-amino acids, the physiological consequence of this switch in N73 specificity remains to be elucidated.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge about eukaryotic aminoacylation fidelity.

claim: D-aminoacyl-tRNAs are discriminated against by other cellular 'chiral checkpoints', namely EF-Tu and ribosome.
source: D-aminoacyl-tRNAs are discriminated against by other cellular 'chiral checkpoints', namely EF-Tu and ribosome (Bhuta et al., 1981; Englander et al., 2015; Pingoud and Urbanke, 1980; Yamane et al., 1981), which together with DTD preclude D-amino acid infiltration into the translational machinery.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on chiral discrimination.

claim: Gly-tRNAAla is not expected to be adequately distinguished from L-Ala-tRNAAla by EF-Tu and ribosome.
source: Since Gly-tRNAAla is not expected to be adequately distinguished from L-Ala-tRNAAla by EF-Tu and ribosome (Dale et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on EF-Tu and ribosome discrimination.

claim: Glycine mischarged on tRNAAla can be misincorporated into the growing polypeptide chain in the absence of DTD.
source: we hypothesized that glycine mischarged on tRNAAla can be misincorporated into the growing polypeptide chain in the absence of DTD
evidence: This hypothesis is tested and confirmed by the GFP reporter assay.

claim: The ability of GFP to fluoresce depends on a key motif (65S/TYG67) in which mutation of the invariant glycine to any other residue abrogates chromophore formation.
source: The ability of GFP to fluoresce depends on a key motif (65S/TYG67) in which mutation of the invariant glycine to any other residue abrogates chromophore formation, resulting in complete loss of fluorescence (Tsien, 1998; Zimmer, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on GFP chromophore formation.

claim: The dtd knockout strain shows GFP fluorescence upon glycine supplementation, indicating misincorporation of glycine in place of alanine.
source: While no GFP fluorescence is observed in cells with the genomic copy of dtd gene (Figure 4b), the dtd knockout strain shows GFP fluorescence upon glycine supplementation, clearly indicating misincorporation of glycine in place of alanine (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the GFP reporter assay shown in Figure 4.

claim: The increase in fluorescence with increasing glycine supplementation in the dtd-null E. coli strain substantiates the increased toxicity upon glycine supplementation.
source: Moreover, the increase in fluorescence with increasing glycine supplementation in the dtd-null E. coli strain substantiates the increased toxicity upon glycine supplementation observed in our recent study (Pawar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-dependent fluorescence in Figure 4c and connected to previous observations.

claim: DTD is not merely a 'recycler' of Gly-tRNAAla, but prevents alanine-to-glycine misincorporation in proteins.
source: These data clearly reveal that DTD is not merely a 'recycler' of Gly-tRNAAla, but prevents alanine-to-glycine misincorporation in proteins and consequent cellular toxicity because A73 and G3•U70 in the substrate enable efficient editing by the enzyme.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the GFP reporter assay showing misincorporation in the absence of DTD.

claim: A73 and G3•U70 in tRNAAla enable efficient editing by DTD.
source: These data clearly reveal that DTD is not merely a 'recycler' of Gly-tRNAAla, but prevents alanine-to-glycine misincorporation in proteins and consequent cellular toxicity because A73 and G3•U70 in the substrate enable efficient editing by the enzyme.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the combined biochemical and in vivo data.

claim: The dichotomy of N73 seen in bacterial tRNAGly and tRNAAla is lacking in Archaea and Eukarya.
source: Intriguingly, our bioinformatic analysis also revealed that the dichotomy of N73 seen in bacterial tRNAGly and tRNAAla is lacking in Archaea and Eukarya
evidence: This is demonstrated by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: G3•U70 wobble base pair in the acceptor stem of tRNAAla is a universal determinant for AlaRS specificity.
source: G3•U70 wobble base pair in the acceptor stem of tRNAAla is a universal determinant for AlaRS specificity (Beebe et al., 2008; Hou and Schimmel, 1988; McClain and Foss, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on AlaRS specificity.

claim: G•U at the third base pair position, or in certain cases even at the fourth base pair level, can result in AlaRS charging non-cognate tRNAs with L-alanine.
source: This specificity is so strict that G•U at the third base pair position, or in certain cases even at the fourth base pair level, can result in AlaRS charging non-cognate tRNAs with L-alanine (Kuncha et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies on AlaRS mischarging.

claim: G3•U70-based discrimination between tRNAGly and tRNAAla by DTD is conserved in Eukarya.
source: We have further shown that G3•U70-based discrimination between tRNAGly and tRNAAla by DTD is also conserved in Eukarya.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the biochemical data with mouse DTD.

claim: DTD must use tRNA elements in a major way to discriminate between two cellular substrates carrying the same amino acid.
source: These findings unequivocally demonstrate the obligatory requirement for DTD to use tRNA elements in a major way to discriminate between two cellular substrates, one essential for protein synthesis and the other a misaminoacylated species, carrying the same amino acid, that is achiral glycine.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing N73 and G3•U70 effects.

claim: The high efficiency of bacterial DTD in clearing Gly-tRNAAla is the plausible reason why it shows significant activity on Gly-tRNAGly.
source: Moreover, the study has also suggested that the high efficiency of bacterial DTD in clearing Gly-tRNAAla is the plausible reason why it shows significant activity on Gly-tRNAGly, albeit at a 1000-fold less efficiency.
evidence: This is speculated based on the trade-off between speed and accuracy.

claim: There is an interesting trade-off between speed and accuracy in DTD's proofreading activity.
source: This points towards an interesting trade-off between speed and accuracy that exists in the case of DTD's proofreading activity, thereby making DTD uniquely distinct from all other known editing enzymes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that DTD acts on both cognate and non-cognate substrates with different efficiencies.

claim: In eukaryotes other mechanisms such as spatiotemporal regulation of expression and cellular compartmentalization of DTD may play role in preventing cognate (Gly-tRNAGly) depletion.
source: It also suggests that in eukaryotes other mechanisms such as spatiotemporal regulation of expression and cellular compartmentalization of DTD may play role in preventing cognate (Gly-tRNAGly) depletion.
evidence: This is speculated based on the lack of N73 discrimination in eukaryotes.

claim: Human DTD has been shown to be enriched in the nuclear envelope region.
source: It is worth mentioning in this context that human DTD has been shown to be enriched in the nuclear envelope region (Zheng et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous localization study.

claim: Acceptor stem based tRNA determinants exist for other standalone proofreading modules such as AlaXs, YbaK and ProXp-ala.
source: Interestingly, such an acceptor stem based tRNA determinants has been shown to exist for other standalone proofreading modules also such as AlaXs, YbaK and ProXp-ala (Bacusmo et al., 2017; Beebe et al., 2008; Das et al., 2014; Vargas-Rodriguez and Musier-Forsyth, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on other editing enzymes.

claim: Bacterial DTD and A/G73-containing tRNAGly or eukaryotic DTD and U/C73-containing tRNAGly are likely to be incompatible.
source: These findings also suggest that bacterial DTD and A/G73-containing tRNAGly or eukaryotic DTD and U/C73-containing tRNAGly are likely to be incompatible.
evidence: This is inferred from the inverted N73 specificities of bacterial and eukaryotic DTD.

claim: The uneven distribution of tRNAs into different discriminator classes based on N73 was used to propose the 'Discriminator Hypothesis' by Donald Crothers about 50 years ago.
source: The uneven, yet interesting, distribution of tRNAs into different discriminator classes based on N73 was used to propose an elegant 'Discriminator Hypothesis' by Donald Crothers about 50 years ago (Crothers et al., 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original Discriminator Hypothesis paper.

claim: The discriminator base classification reflects the partitioning of tRNAs based on the chemical nature of the amino acid to be attached.
source: This classification also reflects the partitioning of tRNAs based on the chemical nature of the amino acid to be attached, that is A73 class includes tRNAs which code for hydrophobic amino acids, while G73-containing tRNAs code for hydrophilic amino acids (Crothers et al., 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Discriminator Hypothesis.

claim: N73 is predominantly a purine across all three domains of life.
source: As can be seen from our current bioinformatic analysis on the discriminator code usage from all three branches of life (Figure 1c), N73 is predominantly a purine.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Factors like RNase P and CCA-adding enzyme have led to purine bias in N73 in all the three domains of life.
source: It has been already noted that factors like RNase P and CCA-adding enzyme have led to purine bias in N73 in all the three domains of life (Figure 1c) (Burkard et al., 1988; Connolly et al., 2004; Giegé et al., 1998; Hamann and Hou, 1995; Hou et al., 2001; Puglisi et al., 1994; Wende et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on RNase P and CCA-adding enzyme.

claim: C73 in prokaryotic tRNAHis is essential to retain G-1 during processing by RNaseP.
source: C73 in prokaryotic tRNAHis is essential to retain G-1 during processing by RNaseP, while in the case of eukaryotic tRNAHis, G-1 is added latter as a post-transcriptional modification (Burkard et al., 1988; Connolly et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on tRNAHis processing.

claim: In eukaryotic tRNAHis, G-1 is added as a post-transcriptional modification.
source: C73 in prokaryotic tRNAHis is essential to retain G-1 during processing by RNaseP, while in the case of eukaryotic tRNAHis, G-1 is added latter as a post-transcriptional modification (Burkard et al., 1988; Connolly et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on tRNAHis maturation.

claim: In tRNACys, U73 is essential for aminoacylation by cysteinyl-tRNA synthetase.
source: In tRNACys, U73 is essential for aminoacylation by cysteinyl-tRNA synthetase (Hamann and Hou, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on CysRS specificity.

claim: CCA-adding enzyme prefers purine as N73 because pyrimidine at that position leads to slow addition of CCA as well as a compromise in the fidelity of CCA addition.
source: Recent evidence shows that CCA-adding enzyme prefers purine as N73 because pyrimidine at that position leads to slow addition of CCA as well as a compromise in the fidelity of CCA addition (Wende et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study on CCA-adding enzyme.

claim: A stronger selection pressure is required to deviate from a purine-based discriminator code.
source: The above examples in conjunction with the current day discriminator code usage (Figure 1c) clearly demonstrate that a stronger selection pressure is required to deviate from a purine-based discriminator code.
evidence: This is inferred from the examples of factors favoring purine at N73 and the observed distribution.

claim: The evolutionary selection pressure exerted by DTD for retention of U73 in bacterial tRNAGly appears stronger than that exerted by other factors like RNase P and CCA-adding enzyme.
source: The current study has elucidated this hitherto unexplained case of bacterial tRNAGly, wherein the evolutionary selection pressure exerted by DTD for retention of U73 appears stronger than that exerted by any of the other aforesaid factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the invariant U73 in bacterial tRNAGly despite factors favoring purine.

claim: Eukaryotes have evolved mechanisms that helped in relieving the selection pressure of keeping U73 in tRNAGly.
